title: Ill in England: when to use a pharmacy, GP, NHS 111, urgent treatment, A&E or 999
summary: How to choose between a pharmacy, GP, NHS 111, an urgent treatment centre, A&E and 999 when you are ill in England, and what each one is for.

# Ill in England: when to use a pharmacy, GP, NHS 111, urgent treatment, A&E or 999

Last updated: 2026-11-27

> This guide covers **England**. Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland each have their own arrangements, with different service names and processes, and we will cover them separately.

If you are used to going straight to a hospital whenever you feel unwell, England may be confusing at first. Here, hospital emergency departments (A&E) are kept for serious situations; everyday minor illnesses and long-term conditions are mainly handled by pharmacies and GPs. In between there is NHS 111, by phone or online, which helps you work out where to go. Each service covers a different part, and once you understand how they divide the work, you won't have to rush from place to place when you are actually ill.

## For a life-threatening emergency, call 999 straight away

This comes first, because it is the one you should not hesitate over.

999 is the emergency number, for when someone's life is at risk. The NHS website gives examples such as serious road accidents, strokes and heart attacks. For a life-threatening emergency, call 999 straight away. If you are not sure whether you need to call 999, you can contact NHS 111, which will help you decide what to do next. [See the official source](#guide-evidence-call-999-or-use-111-if-unsure)

When you call, the call handler will ask where you are, what has happened and for a contact number. Calling 999 does not always mean an ambulance will be sent: the call handler may tell you to go to A&E or somewhere else yourself; if it really is life-threatening, paramedics will be sent. [See the official source](#guide-evidence-what-happens-when-calling-999)

The rest of this guide covers other situations, which is what you will face most of the time.

## Minor illnesses: start with a pharmacy

In England, pharmacies are not just places to buy medicine; the pharmacist is part of the NHS route to care. For common minor illnesses you can walk in and ask, without an appointment.

Since 2024 England has had a service called Pharmacy First. For the seven conditions below, a pharmacist can assess you following a set clinical pathway and, if appropriate, give you some medicines that would otherwise need a prescription, without seeing a GP first:

- sinusitis: aged 12 and over;
- sore throat: aged 5 and over;
- earache caused by a middle ear infection: aged 1 to 17;
- infected insect bite: aged 1 and over;
- impetigo: aged 1 and over;
- shingles: aged 18 and over;
- uncomplicated urinary tract infection (UTI): women aged 16 to 64. [See the official source](#guide-evidence-pharmacy-first-seven-conditions)

For these seven conditions you can go straight to a pharmacy. If the pharmacist thinks your problem is beyond what the pharmacy can deal with, they may send you to a GP or another health service. This is normal triage, not being turned away. [See the official source](#guide-evidence-pharmacy-direct-access-and-onward-referral)

## Need a doctor, but it isn't urgent: contact your GP

Your GP is the doctor at the general practice you are registered with, and handles everyday medical care: symptoms that have dragged on without improving, tests, and adjusting medicines for long-term conditions. In England, for non-urgent problems you generally do not go to a hospital specialist yourself; you see a GP first, and the GP decides whether to refer you to hospital (this is called a referral).

GP practices are usually open from 8am to 6:30pm, Monday to Friday. During these hours you can go in, phone, or contact the practice online through its website or the NHS App. The practice will arrange things according to how serious your problem is and tell you within one working day what happens next: it may ask you to come in that day, or call you first. However, this does not mean you will always be seen the same day. [See the official source](#guide-evidence-gp-contact-hours-and-response)

If you have not registered with a GP yet, see our separate guide on registering with a GP.

## Not sure where to go, or the GP is closed: NHS 111

NHS 111 is not a hospital or a place where you are treated. It is a service that helps you decide what to do next. Use it when you think you need medical help now but are not sure where to go.

There are two ways to use it:

- **online**: at 111.nhs.uk, answer a series of questions about your symptoms and you will be told what to do. The online service is for people aged 5 and over;
- **by phone**: call 111. For children under 5, more complicated problems, or if you already have a care plan, it is better to call. [See the official source](#guide-evidence-nhs-111-online-and-phone)

111 is free and available 24 hours a day. If English is difficult for you, you can ask for an interpreter when you call. [See the official source](#guide-evidence-nhs-111-free-24-hours-interpreter)

After using 111, common outcomes are: being told to go to A&E; being told to go to an urgent treatment centre, sometimes with an arrival time booked for you online; being put in touch with an out-of-hours GP; or arranging for a nurse to call you back, with callbacks prioritised by how serious your symptoms are. 111 can also help if you have an urgent dental problem or have run out of a regular medicine and urgently need more. [See the official source](#guide-evidence-nhs-111-outcomes)

Remember: 111 is not an emergency number. If someone's life is at risk, call 999.

## Urgent, but not life-threatening: an urgent treatment centre

Some problems can't wait for a GP appointment but are not serious enough for A&E, such as sprains, a suspected broken bone, injuries, skin infections or a high temperature. In these cases you can consider an urgent treatment centre (UTC). They can do X-rays and some other tests, and can arrange medicines if you need them. [See the official source](#guide-evidence-utc-conditions-tests-prescriptions)

NHS England has national standards for UTCs: they must be open at least 12 hours a day, 7 days a week; they see both people with appointments and people who walk in; and they treat adults and children of all ages, including children under 2. However, the NHS also recommends using 111 first for urgent problems, and where necessary it can book you an arrival time. At a UTC, people who are more unwell and people with appointments may be seen first. [See the official source](#guide-evidence-utc-national-standards)

Note that things differ from area to area. You may also hear names like walk-in centre or minor injuries unit. These are different types of service left over from the past, and NHS England set UTC standards to bring these differently named services together. But where you live, the name, opening hours and what can be treated may all be different. The easiest approach is to use 111 first, or check what is near you with "Find urgent and emergency care services" on the NHS website. [See the official source](#guide-evidence-utc-legacy-names-and-local-variation)

## A&E: serious injuries and life-threatening emergencies

A&E (Accident and Emergency) is for serious injuries and life-threatening emergencies. It is open 24 hours a day, and you can go directly without an appointment. [See the official source](#guide-evidence-ae-purpose-and-access)

Do not drive yourself there: ask someone to take you, or call 999. Bring any medicines you are taking. [See the official source](#guide-evidence-ae-getting-there)

When you arrive, every patient is assessed first; this is called triage. People are seen in order of how serious their condition is, not in order of arrival. So if you arrived early but see someone who came later go in first, it is usually because their condition is more urgent. The NHS website also says A&E departments are often very busy, and if your condition is not among the most urgent you may have to wait a long time. Waiting is about priorities; it does not mean nobody is looking after you. [See the official source](#guide-evidence-ae-triage-and-waits)

After assessment, if the doctor thinks your situation would be better handled at an urgent treatment centre or by a GP, they may suggest you go there. This is to find a more suitable place for you, not a refusal to treat you. [See the official source](#guide-evidence-ae-redirection-after-assessment)

In England, emergency treatment in A&E is free for everyone (except people who came to the UK specifically to get treatment). You do not need to be registered with a GP or have an NHS number. Urgent treatment that must be given immediately will not be delayed or refused because you cannot pay at the time. If you then need to be admitted to hospital, how charges work depends on your status; that is a separate topic, which we will cover separately. [See the official source](#guide-evidence-ae-charges-and-immediately-necessary-care)

## How to tell 999 and 111 apart

The simplest way to tell them apart:

- **a life-threatening emergency**: call 999;
- **something that needs dealing with soon but does not seem life-threatening**, or you are not sure whether you need to call 999: use NHS 111 to help you decide what to do next.

For a life-threatening emergency, call 999 straight away. If you are not sure whether you need to call 999, you can contact NHS 111, which will help you decide what to do next. [See the official source](#guide-evidence-call-999-or-use-111-if-unsure)

## Evenings and weekends, when the GP is closed

After the GP closes, or at weekends, if you can't wait for the practice to open:

- use 111 first, online or by phone. Depending on your situation, it will send you to an urgent treatment centre, put you in touch with an out-of-hours GP, or tell you to go to A&E;
- A&E is open 24 hours a day, but it is for serious injuries and life-threatening emergencies; [See the official source](#guide-evidence-ae-purpose-and-access)
- if you have run out of a regular medicine and can't wait for the GP to open, you can use the emergency prescription service on 111 online; pharmacies can sometimes give you certain emergency medicines without a prescription, but you may need to pay; [See the official source](#guide-evidence-out-of-hours-emergency-prescriptions)
- if someone's life is at risk, call 999.

## Remember these steps

When you feel unwell, think it through in this order:

1. **Is it a life-threatening emergency?** Call 999. If you are not sure whether you need to call 999, use NHS 111 to help you decide what to do next. [See the official source](#guide-evidence-call-999-or-use-111-if-unsure)
2. **Is it a serious injury or a life-threatening emergency?** If so, go to A&E. [See the official source](#guide-evidence-ae-purpose-and-access)
3. **Urgent, but not life-threatening? Or not sure?** Use 111, which will tell you whether to go to an urgent treatment centre, see an out-of-hours GP or go somewhere else.
4. **Is it a common minor illness?** Ask at a pharmacy first.
5. **Not urgent, but you need a doctor or a referral?** Contact your GP.
